notes: Care Standards Tribunal fitness appeal; Regulation 9 mandatory criteria and inadequate Tribunal reasoning are clearly addressed.

enrichment.short_title: Care home manager registration appeal on fitness under Regulation 9
key_facts: The National Care Standards Commission refused to register Mr Jones as manager of Middlefield House, a residential care home for adults with severe learning disabilities.

The Commission relied on his inadequate knowledge of applicable standards, NMC findings of four counts of professional misconduct at a previous home, and dishonest non-disclosure on his registration application form.
The Care Standards Tribunal allowed Mr Jones's appeal in a finely balanced decision, treating Regulation 9 partly as guidance rather than mandatory criteria.
The Commission appealed on the grounds that the Tribunal misdirected itself on the statutory test of fitness and reached perverse conclusions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal on a point of law from a Care Standards Tribunal decision allowing an appeal against refusal of registration as a care home manager.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Tribunal decision quashed and remitted for reconsideration on the correct legal basis.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 9 of the Care Homes Regulations 2001 provides a mandatory statutory definition of fitness to manage a care home, requiring integrity and good character and necessary qualifications, skills and experience; the Tribunal must address those criteria expressly and give intelligible reasons, including whether NMC misconduct findings bear on integrity and good character and not merely on skills and experience.
legal_issues: Whether Regulation 9 is mandatory guidance or a binding definition of fitness
Whether the Tribunal asked and answered the correct statutory questions
Whether NMC misconduct findings relate to integrity and good character
Whether the burden of proof on appeal lies on the Commission or the applicant

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, Tribunal errors and quashing order are explicit. Burden of proof point was raised but not finally decided.

notes: CCRC sentence reference on licence recall credit; Sharkey principle and section 116 adjustment are straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Credit for custody after administrative licence recall on section 116 sentence
key_facts: Mr Melady was conditionally released on licence from a two-and-a-half-year sentence but committed further offences during the licence period.
His licence was administratively revoked and he served 125 days in custody as a licence revokee before being sentenced for the new offences.
The Crown Court ordered 315 days of the original sentence to be served before the three-year term for the new offences but made no allowance for the 125 days already served.
Section 67 did not permit the Prison Service to deduct the licence-recall period from either the section 116 order or the new sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Sentence appeal following a Criminal Cases Review Commission reference after leave to appeal had been refused by the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the section 116 period reduced from 315 days to 65 days to reflect 125 days already served in custody after licence recall.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant has already served time in custody following administrative revocation of a licence before being sentenced under section 116 for offences committed during the unexpired portion of the earlier sentence, the court should ordinarily make allowance for that time; for a short-term prisoner each day in custody counts as two days for this purpose.
legal_issues: How time spent in custody after administrative licence recall should be treated on sentencing under section 116
Whether section 67 permits credit for licence-recall custody
Application of the principle in Sharkey to licence revocations
linked_authorities: Sharkey [2001] 1 Cr App R 409

confidence.notes: Facts, arithmetic adjustment and Sharkey principle are clearly stated in a short judgment.

notes: Long TCC trial on samosa pastry production line; contractual and tort claims against Rondo fail, nominal damages against Frampton only.

enrichment.short_title: Filobake samosa pastry production line equipment dispute
key_facts: Filobake Ltd, a joint venture between the Charilaou and Pittalis families, sought to expand production of prepared samosa pastry using a new automated production line.
Rondo Ltd supplied sheeting and related equipment and recommended Frampton Ltd to provide an oven and cooler as part of the New Line.
Filobake claimed the line failed to produce acceptable samosa pastry and sued Rondo for breach of contract and negligence and Frampton for breach of contract.
Filobake's damages case depended on identifying marginal costs of the New Line, but its accounting allocations were found unreliable and not to reflect true marginal costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of claims for breach of contract, implied terms and negligence arising from supply and installation of bakery production equipment.
enrichment.outcome: Claim against Rondo dismissed in its entirety; claim against Frampton succeeds only for nominal damages of £2 for breach of the implied term that the oven was of satisfactory quality due to a belt tensioning defect.
enrichment.ratio: Rondo's obligations were limited to supplying listed components of satisfactory quality capable of producing pastry to Filobake's specified recipe; it did not contractually or tortiously guarantee Frampton's oven and cooler or owe duties to advise on mixers, packaging or freezing techniques; Filobake failed to prove substantial damages because its cost allocation exercise did not identify true marginal costs of the New Line.
legal_issues: Scope of Rondo's contractual obligations under the Final Quotation
Whether implied terms as to fitness for purpose and compatibility arose
Whether Rondo owed duties of care for pure economic loss or to volunteer advice
Whether Frampton breached the implied term of satisfactory quality
Assessment of Filobake's loss and marginal costs

notes: Youth court remittal of indictable-only offence; section 9 limits and section 142 rescission analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Unlawful youth court remittal of indictable-only offence for sentence
key_facts: Richard Denny was charged with attempted robbery at age 17 but was not tried for over a year and was convicted after turning 18.
Acton Youth Court remitted him to the adult magistrates' court for sentence under section 9 of the 2000 Act.
Attempted robbery is triable only on indictment for an adult, so the adult court had no sentencing jurisdiction.
Denny sought judicial review to prevent the youth court rescinding the remittal under section 142, while the prosecution argued the remittal was inherently unlawful.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of youth court remittal and related questions about rescission under section 142 of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant's application refused; remittal order quashed and matter directed to be listed in the youth court for sentence as soon as possible.
enrichment.ratio: Section 9 of the 2000 Act cannot properly be used to remit a young offender to an adult magistrates' court for sentence where the offence would be triable only on indictment if committed by an adult, because the adult court would have no power to sentence; such a remittal is legally defective and should be quashed, and a remittal under section 9 is an order made when dealing with an offender capable of rescission under section 142 while the youth court remains seised.
legal_issues: Whether section 9 permits remittal for sentence of indictable-only offences
Whether an unlawful remittal should be quashed or merely declared defective
Whether section 142 applies to a section 9 remittal order
When the youth court ceases to be seised after remittal

confidence.notes: Statutory construction, quashing order and guidance to youth courts are explicit in the judgment.

notes: Gypsy Green Belt site enforcement; section 178 use after section 187B injunction and Housing Act duties clearly analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Gypsy Green Belt site enforcement by section 178 after County Court injunction
key_facts: Gypsy families occupied Wolvey Road in the Green Belt without planning permission and enforcement action followed refused planning applications and a upheld enforcement notice.
The council obtained a County Court injunction under section 187B requiring vacation by 31 December 2003, which was not complied with.
The council then decided to enforce by entering the land under section 178 rather than pursuing committal proceedings.
Claimants applied for judicial review shortly before planned eviction, asserting late homelessness applications under the Housing Act 1996 and cultural objections to bricks-and-mortar accommodation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a local authority decision to exercise section 178 enforcement powers after obtaining a County Court planning injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; declaration that use of section 178 is lawful, subject to reasonable consideration of homelessness duties and individual circumstances before eviction is implemented.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority may lawfully use section 178 to enforce planning control even after obtaining a section 187B injunction where committal would not clear the site; Article 6 is not engaged because enforcement follows planning decisions already made; however, a late homelessness application under the Housing Act 1996 should have been specifically considered before fixing immediate eviction, though housing duties do not permit indefinite unlawful occupation.
legal_issues: Whether section 178 may be used after section 187B injunction proceedings
Whether Article 6 ECHR requires a further hearing before section 178 enforcement
Interaction of planning enforcement with homelessness duties under the Housing Act 1996
Whether the council properly considered last-minute homelessness applications
linked_authorities: South Buckinghamshire DC v Porter
R (Margaret Price) v Carmarthenshire County Council [2003] EWHC 42 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Main legal conclusions on section 178, Article 6 and Housing Act interaction are clear. Timing of future enforcement is left to the council.

notes: SEND Tribunal disability strike-out appeal; Regulation 44 procedure limits and substantial-effect test errors are clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: SEND Tribunal strike-out of disability discrimination claim

statutes_considered.title: Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal (General Provisions and Disability Claims Procedure) Regulations 2002

key_facts: Parents brought a disability discrimination claim against Rushmoor School on behalf of their son MH, who had complex learning and behavioural difficulties including features of Asperger's syndrome.
The school applied under regulation 44 to strike out the claim on grounds including that MH was not a disabled person within the DDA 1995.
The SEND Tribunal struck out the claim after analysing the evidence and finding the adverse effects of MH's impairment were not substantial.
Parents appealed to the High Court on the legal test for disability, adequacy of reasons, and fairness of using strike-out procedure for a disputed preliminary issue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 against a SEND Tribunal decision striking out a disability discrimination claim.
enrichment.outcome: Tribunal decision quashed and remitted; costs of the appeal awarded to the parents.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 44 strike-out is apt for manifestly unfounded claims but not for detailed disputed fact-finding on disability; the statutory test of substantial adverse effect on normal day-to-day activities means more than minor or trivial and requires focus on what the claimant cannot do or can only do with difficulty, not on academic achievements or things he can still do; the Tribunal erred in applying the test and in treating strike-out as a full preliminary issue determination.
legal_issues: Proper use of regulation 44 strike-out in SEND disability claims
Meaning of substantial adverse effect under section 1 DDA 1995
Whether the Tribunal made adequate findings on impairment and adverse effect
Fairness of determining disability as a preliminary issue on the papers

Leonard v Southern Derbyshire Chamber of Commerce [2001] IRLR 9

confidence.notes: Legal test, procedural criticism and quashing order are clearly reasoned. The court did not decide whether MH is disabled on the merits.

notes: Anonymised restraint-order proceedings; open judgment on jurisdiction under section 77 CJA 1988 is detailed but merits of payment to creditor were decided in private.

enrichment.short_title: Restraint order jurisdiction to pay trade creditors before confiscation
key_facts: A without-notice restraint order was made under section 77 over the assets of an individual and a company he controlled, with a receiver appointed.
A trade creditor claimed £873,972 for goods supplied and applied to vary the restraint order to permit payment.
The prosecutor argued the court had no jurisdiction to authorise payment to general creditors in priority to the Crown's confiscation interest.
The open judgment addressed only the jurisdiction point; the application was dismissed on the merits in a private judgment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications to vary a section 77 restraint order and for receiver directions in pending criminal confiscation proceedings, with an open judgment on jurisdiction only.
enrichment.outcome: Open judgment holds the court has jurisdiction to vary a restraint order to permit payment to creditors before conviction; the creditor's application was dismissed on the facts in the private portion of the judgment.
enrichment.ratio: Before conviction, section 77 confers a broad discretion to vary restraint orders and permit payments including to trade creditors; section 82(2)'s requirement to exercise powers with a view to preserving realisable property introduces flexibility rather than an absolute bar on paying creditors, and re W was wrongly decided to the extent it held the Crown always has priority over general creditors at the restraint stage.
legal_issues: Whether a restraint order under section 77 can be varied to pay bona fide trade creditors
Construction of section 82(2) and section 82(6) of the 1988 Act
Whether re W should be followed on Crown priority before confiscation
Application of re Peters and Mareva analogy to restraint orders

notes: Trade mark counterfeit conviction appeal; Johnstone trade mark use direction defect and unsafe conviction analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe conviction for selling counterfeit Boss and Polo sweatshirts
key_facts: James Isaac, a market trader, sold sweatshirts bearing Boss and Polo signs for £3 each; the goods were inferior counterfeits not genuine Hugo Boss or Ralph Lauren items.
He was convicted of two counts of selling goods bearing signs identical to registered trade marks contrary to section 92(1)(b).
Counsel agreed draft jury directions referring to use in the course of trade and prejudicing the function of the trade mark, but the defence later appealed on the adequacy of the directions.
The Court of Appeal held the directions did not clearly require proof that the sign was used as an indication of trade origin as explained in R v Johnstone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge in a trade marks Act 1994 prosecution.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed; application for retrial refused.
enrichment.ratio: A section 92 offence requires proof that the offending sign was used as an indication of trade origin; jury directions must state this ingredient clearly, not merely ask whether use was in the course of trade or prejudiced the trade mark's function; where agreed draft directions are inaccurate, counsel cannot later invite the court to treat them as an incomplete template.
legal_issues: Whether section 92 requires proof of trade mark use as indication of origin
Adequacy of jury directions on infringement and section 92(5) defence
Effect of counsel-agreed draft directions on appeal
Whether a retrial should be ordered

confidence.notes: Direction defect, Johnstone principles and quashing order are clearly explained. Retrial refusal reasons are also stated.

notes: Interim detailed assessment directions only; CFA backdating and fraud allegations remain for later preliminary hearings.

enrichment.short_title: Group litigation costs directions on disputed CFA backdating and fraud
key_facts: Over 200 claimants in a group nuisance claim against Biffa Waste Services over a Merthyr Tydfil landfill were mediated to settlement with costs to be assessed.
Generic and individual bills exceeding £2 million were served; many claims were funded by CFAs dated in 2001 though solicitors accept those dates reflect file-opening dates not signing dates.
Defendants alleged the CFAs were backdated and amounted to attempted fraud by claimant solicitors; claimants contended oral retainers preceded written CFAs and the agreements are enforceable.
Six preliminary issues were identified including CFA validity, misconduct penalties, proportionality, success fees and costs orders for discontinuing claimants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reserved judgment on directions for detailed assessment of generic costs and an interim costs certificate application in the SCCO.
enrichment.outcome: Reference to a High Court Judge refused; limited disclosure to Costs Judge only ordered; further information on CFA execution dates required; cross-examination application dismissed as premature; permission to appeal refusal to refer granted provisionally.
enrichment.ratio: Allegations of CFA backdating and solicitor fraud in a large detailed assessment do not automatically require reference to a High Court Judge where the SCCO can determine preliminary issues and apply CPR 44.14; attendance notes and correspondence should not ordinarily be disclosed to the paying party unless a genuine issue of enforceability is raised, though documents may be produced first to the Costs Judge under Hollins v Russell principles.
legal_issues: Whether preliminary issues on CFA validity and alleged fraud should be referred to a High Court Judge
Scope of disclosure of CFAs, attendance notes and ATE correspondence in costs assessment
Whether cross-examination of signing solicitors should be ordered now
What further information must be provided on CFA execution dates
Whether the court's jurisdiction over solicitor misconduct is limited to CPR 44.14 in assessment proceedings

notes: Bank possession and overreaching dispute; resulting trust claim rejected and HRA non-retrospectivity clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Bank possession claim defeating wife's alleged beneficial interest
key_facts: NatWest Bank held a second charge over a leasehold family home securing partnership debts of SND Wholesalers owed by the registered proprietors, Navtej and Anil Malhan.
Anil's wife Puneeta claimed she contributed £31,000 to the purchase price and held a 55.4% beneficial interest under a resulting or constructive trust.
She was in actual occupation when the second charge was created and argued her interest was an overriding interest and that overreaching violated Articles 8 and 14 ECHR and Article 1 Protocol 1.
Accounting records supporting her contribution claim had been destroyed by fire and key documentary evidence was missing or uncorroborated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of a wife's counterclaim in bank possession proceedings transferred from the County Court.
enrichment.outcome: Counterclaim dismissed; Puneeta failed to establish a beneficial interest and there is no defence to possession; matter to return to Reading County Court for possession order.
enrichment.ratio: A spouse claiming a resulting trust must prove contributions to the purchase on the balance of probabilities; where purchase funds came from the family partnership without reliable ledger evidence of a personal credit, no equitable interest is established; even if such an interest existed, registered proprietors had power to create the charge and overreaching under section 2(1) LPA 1925 would defeat the occupier's interest; the Human Rights Act 1998 does not apply retrospectively to overreaching occurring in 1994.
legal_issues: Whether Puneeta established a resulting or constructive trust by financial contribution
Whether her equitable interest was an overriding interest under section 70(1)(g)
Whether section 2(1) LPA 1925 overreached her interest on creation of the second charge
Whether overreaching discriminated under Article 14 with Article 8 or Protocol 1 Article 1
Whether the Human Rights Act 1998 applies to pre-2000 dispositions
